findings.lesson_text: The Bible also teaches: ‘Faith without action is dead’ (James 2:26)
findings.issue: The quote ‘Faith without action is dead’ is attributed to James 2:26, but James 2:26 (NIV) actually reads ‘As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.’ The phrase matching the lesson’s wording is James 2:17: ‘faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead.’ The verse number is wrong.
findings.canonical_truth: James 2:26 NIV: ‘As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.’ The lesson’s quoted wording corresponds to James 2:17 NIV: ‘In the same way, faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead.’

findings.lesson_text: The Bible also teaches: ‘Faith without action is dead’ (James 2:26)
findings.issue: Identical error to the Unity version of this lesson. James 2:26 does not say ‘Faith without action is dead.’ That wording belongs to James 2:17. James 2:26 makes a different analogy (the body without the spirit).
findings.canonical_truth: James 2:26 NIV: ‘As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.’ James 2:17 NIV: ‘In the same way, faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead.’

findings.lesson_text: Satisfaction theory: Human sin offended God’s honour and justice. Only a perfect sacrifice could satisfy God’s justice. Jesus, being sinless, was the only one who could offer this perfect payment. This view is associated with Anselm of Canterbury and is common in Catholic theology.
findings.issue: Calling Anselm’s satisfaction theory ‘common in Catholic theology’ is misleadingly grouped alongside the implication that penal substitution (the view described just before in the lesson) is also Catholic. Penal substitution is a distinctly Protestant doctrine originating with Luther and Calvin; it is NOT the Catholic view. Anselm’s satisfaction theory (honour/debt model) is indeed the dominant Catholic/Thomistic atonement framework, but it differs from Protestant penal substitution. The lesson risks students conflating the two as both being Catholic.
findings.canonical_truth: Anselm’s satisfaction theory (sin violates God’s honour; Christ’s death pays the honour-debt) is the foundational Catholic atonement model, developed further by Aquinas. Penal substitution (Christ bears God’s penal wrath) is primarily Protestant, originating with Luther and Calvin. The two are distinct. Source: Wikipedia ‘Satisfaction theory of atonement’ and ‘Penal substitution’.

findings.lesson_text: Satisfaction theory: Human sin offended God’s honour and justice. Only a perfect sacrifice could satisfy God’s justice. Jesus, being sinless, was the only one who could offer this perfect payment. This view is associated with Anselm of Canterbury and is common in Catholic theology.
findings.issue: Identical doctrinal framing issue as the AQA version. The lesson implies that the preceding penal substitution view and the satisfaction view are both common in Catholic theology, which is incorrect. Penal substitution is a Protestant doctrine; Anselm’s satisfaction theory is Catholic.
findings.canonical_truth: Penal substitution is distinctly Protestant (Luther, Calvin). Anselm’s satisfaction theory is the foundational Catholic atonement model. The two differ in mechanism: satisfaction pays an honour-debt; penal substitution pays a penalty.

findings.lesson_text: ‘Whoever believes in me shall have eternal life’ (John 6:47)
findings.issue: The lesson presents this as a direct quotation of John 6:47 in NIV, but the NIV text of John 6:47 reads: ‘Very truly I tell you, the one who believes has eternal life.’ The lesson’s wording (‘Whoever believes in me shall have eternal life’) more closely resembles John 6:40 NIV (‘everyone who looks to the Son and believes in him shall have eternal life’). The verse is misquoted and the phrasing is drawn from a different verse.
findings.canonical_truth: John 6:47 NIV: ‘Very truly I tell you, the one who believes has eternal life.’ John 6:40 NIV: ‘For my Father’s will is that everyone who looks to the Son and believes in him shall have eternal life.’ Neither verse says ‘Whoever believes in me shall have eternal life’ exactly.

findings.lesson_title: The Nature of God & the Trinity
findings.issue: The NIV 2011 translation of Luke 1:37 reads ‘For no word from God will ever fail.’ — not ‘Nothing is impossible with God.’ The quoted wording is from the KJV/NKJV (‘with God nothing shall be impossible’) or NLT (‘nothing is impossible with God’). As StudyVault content is otherwise NIV-aligned, citing a non-NIV rendering without attribution is a translation mismatch.
findings.canonical_truth: Luke 1:37 NIV 2011: ‘For no word from God will ever fail.’ Luke 1:37 KJV: ‘For with God nothing shall be impossible.’ The lesson uses KJV/NLT wording but attributes the verse without naming the translation.

findings.canonical_truth: Luke 1:37 NIV 2011: ‘For no word from God will ever fail.’ KJV: ‘For with God nothing shall be impossible.’

findings.lesson_title: Life After Death and the Seven Sacraments
findings.lesson_text: Jesus promises: ‘In my Father’s house are many rooms’ (John 14:2)
findings.issue: The phrasing ‘In my Father’s house are many rooms’ is the ESV translation. The NIV 2011 reads ‘My Father’s house has many rooms.’ The lesson presents the ESV wording without translation attribution.
findings.canonical_truth: John 14:2 NIV: ‘My Father’s house has many rooms.’ John 14:2 ESV: ‘In my Father’s house are many rooms.’ The difference is stylistic and does not change the meaning, but the NIV wording differs from what is quoted.

findings.lesson_text: Jesus warns against ‘babbling on like pagans’ (Matthew 6:7)
findings.issue: The NIV reads ‘do not keep on babbling like pagans’ at Matthew 6:7. The lesson’s phrasing ‘babbling on like pagans’ is the Berean Standard Bible (BSB) rendering. The meaning is equivalent but the wording does not match the NIV.
findings.canonical_truth: Matthew 6:7 NIV: ‘And when you pray, do not keep on babbling like pagans, for they think they will be heard because of their many words.’ BSB: ‘And when you pray, do not babble on like pagans.’
